opus-5.5.text:
I think they're broadly credible, actually. If you look at OpenAI's track record, their revenue has grown very quickly, roughly tripling year over year, and their internal projections haven't been wildly off in the past. The figure that circulated for 2025 was somewhere around $12 to $13 billion, up from around $4 billion in 2024. That's an aggressive number, but it's not out of line with what we've already seen.

The main driver is still ChatGPT subscriptions. The user base has been growing very fast, and a meaningful fraction of those users pay. Then there's the API business and enterprise deals on top of that. So when you decompose the forecast into pieces, user growth, conversion rates, average revenue per user, none of the individual assumptions seem crazy to me.

Where I'd be more skeptical is the longer-range projections, the ones that have them reaching $100 billion or more by the end of the decade. Those depend on things that haven't happened yet: agents that can do substantial economically valuable work, new product categories, maybe advertising or commerce. I actually think AI could eventually generate far more revenue than that, but the timing is very uncertain, and it's not obvious OpenAI captures most of it rather than competitors or customers.

So for 2025 specifically, I'd say the estimate is plausible and probably not far off. Companies in this position have some incentive to be optimistic because they're raising enormous amounts of capital. But the near-term numbers are tied to real, observable trends, so I wouldn't discount them much. The uncertainty compounds the further out you go.

r001.rationale: It says OpenAI’s revenue has been roughly tripling year over year and gives a 2025 projection of $12–13 billion, up from about $4 billion in 2024, presenting the forecast as consistent with that past growth.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're fairly credible, actually, at least in the sense that revenue is one of the few things here you can't really fudge. The numbers that have been reported, something on the order of twelve or thirteen billion dollars for 2025, roughly tripling from the year before, those are consistent with what we can observe from the outside. ChatGPT has hundreds of millions of weekly users, a meaningful fraction of them pay twenty dollars a month, enterprise deals are getting signed, and API usage keeps growing. If you do some rough back-of-the-envelope accounting on subscribers times price plus API volume, you land in roughly the right neighborhood. So I don't think they're making those numbers up.

What I'm more skeptical of is the forward-looking projections, the stuff about tens or hundreds of billions by the end of the decade. Those depend on assumptions about continued adoption, about pricing power, about agents actually becoming useful enough that businesses pay a lot more per seat than they do today. Those are the real uncertainties. Historically, the growth in AI revenue has been fast but it hasn't been nearly as fast as the growth in compute spending, and that gap is the thing to watch. OpenAI is committing to enormous amounts of infrastructure, and the revenue has to grow much faster than it has so far for that to pencil out.

The other thing I'd flag is that revenue and profitability are very different questions. They're spending more than they take in, and the question of what their unit economics look like, how much the inference actually costs relative to what people pay, is much less transparent. So I'd say believe the top-line revenue, be more careful with the extrapolations, and be quite uncertain about the margins.

r001.rationale: The response says 2025 revenue is roughly tripling from the prior year, but it does not identify 2023-to-2024 growth or say the 2025 projection continues that growth rate.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between whether the revenue estimate is plausible and whether we should be confident in it. I can imagine OpenAI’s revenue growing very quickly, but I wouldn’t put much weight on a precise forecast without knowing the assumptions behind it. Are they expecting more paying users, higher spending per user, or a big increase in API usage? Those are different bets.

And revenue alone doesn’t tell you whether the business is sustainable. You also need to know how much it costs to serve those customers. So I’d treat the estimate as a plausible scenario, rather than something we should take for granted.

r001.rationale: The response says revenue could grow quickly but does not identify the 2025 projection as continuing roughly threefold annual growth from 2023 to 2024.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between whether the revenue forecast is plausible and what it tells us about the business. I can imagine OpenAI seeing very rapid revenue growth in 2025. There’s clearly a lot of demand, and they have several ways to monetize it: consumer subscriptions, enterprise customers, and API usage. But I wouldn’t put much confidence in a precise number without knowing the assumptions behind it.

For example, are they projecting actual revenue over the year, or an annualized run rate at the end of the year? Those can be very different when a business is growing quickly. And how much of the growth depends on new products or improvements in the models?

So I’d take the estimates seriously as a possible outcome, but not treat them as established facts. And even if they hit the revenue target, that leaves a separate question about the costs of serving that demand and developing the next generation of models.

r001.rationale: The response says rapid 2025 revenue growth is plausible, but it does not identify the roughly threefold growth from 2023 to 2024 or say that the 2025 projection continues that pace.
